explanations.explanation: Not quite, baker. The text says she “gave birth to a son.” (Exodus 2:2) That matters, because Pharaoh, king of Egypt, had ordered that the Hebrew sons be thrown into the Nile (Exodus 1:22). So this baby boy was born right into the danger.

That's it, friend. The text says she “gave birth to a son.” (Exodus 2:2) Pharaoh, king of Egypt, had ordered that the Hebrew sons be thrown into the Nile (Exodus 1:22). So a baby boy was born right into the middle of that order.
Yes, friend. The text says “…she hid him for three months.” (Exodus 2:2) Three whole months. I couldn't keep a cookie box shut for three minutes, and she kept a baby tucked away that long.
Not this time, baker. The text says “…she hid him for three months.” (Exodus 2:2) So she did manage it, and for a good long while. I'd have been a nervous wreck by day two.
You got it, baker. The text says she “got him a papyrus basket.” (Exodus 2:3) Then she coated it with tar and pitch. That's one small basket doing a very big job.
Close on the water part, friend. But the text says she got him a papyrus basket, not a boat. (Exodus 2:3) She coated that basket with tar and pitch. It was small enough to tuck in among the reeds.

Not a jar, baker. The text says she got him a papyrus basket. (Exodus 2:3) Then she coated it with tar and pitch before she set the child inside. A baby in a jar sounds like a very different story, and thankfully it isn't this one.

That's right, baker. She set the basket “among the reeds along the bank of the Nile.” (Exodus 2:3) Reeds are the tall plants that grow at the water's edge. She put the basket right in them, close to the bank.

Not rocks, friend. The text says she set the basket “among the reeds along the bank of the Nile.” (Exodus 2:3) Reeds are the tall plants that grow right at the water's edge. Rocks would make for a pretty bumpy spot for a baby.

Not boats, baker. The text says she set the basket “among the reeds along the bank of the Nile.” (Exodus 2:3) The basket was the only thing floating around in this story. The reeds were the neighbors.

explanations.answer: To see what would happen to him
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The text says his sister “stood at a distance to see what would happen to him.” (Exodus 2:4) She stayed close enough to watch but not so close to draw attention. I think she watched that basket like I watch the oven timer.

explanations.answer: To wait for their mother to return
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that, friend. It says his sister stood at a distance “to see what would happen to him.” (Exodus 2:4) Nothing there says she was waiting on their mother. Her eyes were on the basket.

explanations.answer: To keep strangers away from the reeds
explanations.explanation: Not quite, baker. The text gives her reason: she stood at a distance “to see what would happen to him.” (Exodus 2:4) She was watching, not guarding. The text never says she chased anyone off.

Not this time, friend. When Pharaoh's daughter, the daughter of Egypt's king, saw the basket among the reeds, she sent her maidservant to retrieve it. (Exodus 2:5) So she didn't leave it there at all. That basket was getting picked up.

That's right, baker. Pharaoh's daughter, the daughter of Egypt's king, saw the basket and “sent her maidservant to retrieve it.” (Exodus 2:5) She didn't walk past it. A basket in the reeds got her attention.

Yes, baker. The text says “…the little boy was crying. So she had compassion on him…” (Exodus 2:6) A crying baby changed the whole moment for her. And she was the daughter of the very king who gave the order about the Hebrew sons (Exodus 1:22).
Not anger, friend. The text says “…the little boy was crying. So she had compassion on him…” (Exodus 2:6) She opened that basket and her heart went soft. That's the surprise in this scene.
Not fear, baker. The text says she “had compassion on him.” (Exodus 2:6) The text doesn't say she was afraid of anything. She saw a crying baby and felt for him.
You got it, baker. She said, “This is one of the Hebrew children.” (Exodus 2:6) She knew exactly whose baby this was. And she still had compassion on him.
Not Egyptian, friend. She said, “This is one of the Hebrew children.” (Exodus 2:6) She knew the baby wasn't from an Egyptian family. She felt compassion for him anyway.
Not Midianite, baker. The text has her say, “This is one of the Hebrew children.” (Exodus 2:6) Hebrew is the word she used. Midianite doesn't show up anywhere in this scene.

explanations.answer: Call a Hebrew woman to nurse him
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The sister asked, “Shall I go and call one of the Hebrew women to nurse the child for you?” (Exodus 2:7) She had the whole idea ready. I just hope my own big ideas land as well as hers did.

explanations.answer: Carry the basket up to the palace
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. The sister asked, “Shall I go and call one of the Hebrew women to nurse the child for you?” (Exodus 2:7) The text says nothing about a palace or carrying a basket. Her offer was to go and get a nurse.

explanations.answer: Watch the baby while she bathes
explanations.explanation: Not that one, baker. The sister asked, “Shall I go and call one of the Hebrew women to nurse the child for you?” (Exodus 2:7) She offered to find a nurse for the baby. Babysitting during a bath isn't in the text.
Yes, baker. The text says “the girl went and called the boy's mother.” (Exodus 2:8) She went and got the one woman who already knew this baby best. I think that was one fast walk back to the river.
Not Puah, friend. She was one of the Hebrew midwives the king of Egypt spoke to (Exodus 1:15). But in this scene the girl “called the boy's mother.” (Exodus 2:8) Puah never shows up here.
Not Shiphrah, baker. She was one of the Hebrew midwives the king of Egypt spoke to (Exodus 1:15). But in this scene the girl “called the boy's mother.” (Exodus 2:8) The mother is the one who came.

Yes, friend. Pharaoh's daughter said, “Take this child and nurse him for me, and I will pay your wages.” (Exodus 2:9) A mother gets her own baby back and a paycheck on top of it. Now THAT is a good day at work.

Not this time, baker. Pharaoh's daughter said, “Take this child and nurse him for me, and I will pay your wages.” (Exodus 2:9) So she did promise wages. The mother would be paid to care for her own son.

That's right, baker. The text says, “…he became her son.” (Exodus 2:10) The boy was brought to Pharaoh's daughter after he had grown older. So a Hebrew baby ends up with a place in Pharaoh's own family.
Not a servant, friend. The text says, “…he became her son.” (Exodus 2:10) That's a very different title. The text doesn't say anything about a servant's job.

explanations.answer: He returns to the house of Levi
explanations.explanation: Not that one, baker. The text says that when his mother brought him to Pharaoh's daughter, “…he became her son.” (Exodus 2:10) The text doesn't say he went back to the house of Levi here. He became her son.

You got it, baker. She named him Moses and explained, “I drew him out of the water.” (Exodus 2:10) The name comes from that moment at the river. A basket in the reeds, and a boy pulled out of the Nile.
Not the desert, friend. She named him Moses and explained, “I drew him out of the water.” (Exodus 2:10) This whole scene happens at the Nile. There's not a grain of sand in it.
Not mountains, baker. She named him Moses and explained, “I drew him out of the water.” (Exodus 2:10) Everything here happens down at the river. I'd stay near the water for this one.
